lines.text: A floating-point number needs three things. A sign, an exponent, and a mantissa.
The exponent says how big or small the number can be. The mantissa says how finely you can pin it down.
FP32 spends thirty-two bits on that. Eight for the exponent, twenty-three for the mantissa, one for the sign.
Halve it and you halve the mantissa first. FP16 keeps five exponent bits and ten mantissa bits.
Keep going and you hit the real problem. The exponent runs out of room before the mantissa does.
FP8 splits the difference two ways. E4M3 has four exponent bits and three mantissa bits. E5M2 has five and two.
E4M3 has more precision and less range. E5M2 has more range and less precision.
Which one you want depends on whether you are storing a weight or an activation.
Then there is the clever part. You can shrink it to four bits. One sign, two exponent, one mantissa.
That is so little precision that one shared scale for a whole block of numbers would destroy them.
So the format stores a small scale factor alongside the block, and that scale is different for every group of values.
Four bits per number, and the block keeps its meaning.
That is how four-bit weights survive at all. The scale saves what one mantissa bit cannot hold.
